extracted.intended_audience: Researchers/Principal Investigators applying for NLM/NIH grants
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how NLM/NIH grant applications are scored, how reviewers assign criterion and impact/priority scores, what those scores mean for funding likelihood, and what written feedback and follow-up requests applicants receive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact/priority score
rubrics_metrics.description: After discussing an application, members of the review group privately vote a numerical impact/priority score from 1 to 9, where 1 is best. The normalized average of all reviewer impact/priority scores constitutes the final impact/priority score. Impact scores run from 10 to 90, where 10 is best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally speaking, impact/priority scores of 10 to 30 are most likely to be funded; scores between 31 and 45 might be funded; scores greater than 46 are rarely funded. (Historical note: before 2009 NIH used a different score system with final scores from 100 to 500, where 100 was best.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion scores (core NIH review criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers assign a criterion score from 1 to 9, where 1 is best, to each core NIH review criterion (significance, investigator, innovation, approach, environment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These criterion scores are provided to assist applicants in understanding the strengths and weaknesses of their application and to assist program staff in funding decisions. Criterion scores are not used to calculate the final impact/priority score.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding decision factors beyond score
rubrics_metrics.description: A favorable impact/priority score does not by itself guarantee funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All grant awards depend on availability of funds, relevance to NLM priorities, and the balance of grants in NLM's grant portfolio. Applicants should consult success-rate data for additional context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability/access to impact/priority scores
rubrics_metrics.description: Impact scores are typically available within a few days after the applications are reviewed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Log into your NIH eRA Commons PI account to see your impact/priority score.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary Statement: timing and content of written evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Approximately 4 weeks after your application is reviewed, a written evaluation called the Summary Statement will be posted in the NIH eRA Commons. The Summary Statement is compiled by the Scientific Review Officer (SRO) who ran the review meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In addition to administrative information, it contains the written critiques prepared by the assigned reviewers and recommendations regarding budget and human subject considerations. If the application received full discussion, the Summary Statement also includes a resume and summary of the discussion written by the SRO. Applicants can read and download the Summary Statement from eRA Commons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request for additional information (not an award notice)
rubrics_metrics.description: If NLM requests additional information after review, this does not mean the grant will be funded; it means the application is under consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applications with impact/priority scores that fall within the fundable range are sent to the second level of review. For those applications, NLM Grants Management staff may request documentation such as updated 'other support' for key participants, the status of Institutional Review Board action, and certification that key personnel have received training in the protection of human subjects. Such a request for additional information is not an award notice.
